title: Review: Potential difference and emf; Electrical power and energy; Series and parallel circuits; Kirchhoff's laws
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: EL05-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL06-1#t3 term and clue written for the game; EL06-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; EL02-1#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: EL02-1#N.13a, EL05-1#N.5, EL06-1#N.4, EL02-1#N.3a, EL05-1#N.3, EL06-1#N.10a, EL02-1#N.6, EL05-1#N.10b, EL06-1#N.14, EL05-1#N.11a, EL06-1#N.2, EL06-1#N.11. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Power
items.clue: Rate of energy transfer, which can be found from I²R.

items.label: Ammeter
items.clue: Instrument placed in series; an ideal one has zero resistance.

items.label: Open circuit
items.clue: A gap anywhere in a loop, so that no current flows in that loop.

items.label: Volt
items.clue: Unit meaning 1 J transferred for each coulomb passing between two places.

questions.stem: A battery of emf 12 V drives a steady current of 40 A through a starter motor for 1.5 s. How much energy does the battery transfer to the charge that passes through it in this time?
questions.explanation: Charge: q = It = 40 × 1.5 = 60 C. Each coulomb gains 12 J, so energy = emf × q = 12 × 60 = 720 J.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.25 A flows in a 24 Ω resistor for 2.0 minutes. How much energy is dissipated in the resistor?
questions.explanation: Power = I²R = 0.25² × 24 = 1.5 W. Energy = power × time = 1.5 W × 120 s = 180 J.

questions.stem: A 9.0 V supply of negligible internal resistance is connected to three resistors in series. The potential differences across two of them are 2.0 V and 4.5 V. What is the potential difference across the third resistor?
questions.explanation: Energy is conserved round the loop: the three potential differences add up to the supply's 9.0 V. 9.0 − 2.0 − 4.5 = 2.5 V.

questions.stem: A steady current of 0.50 A flows through a small electric motor for 2.0 minutes. In this time, 360 J of energy is transferred from electrical energy to other forms in the motor. What is the potential difference across the motor?

The potential difference across an ohmic resistor is increased so that the current in the resistor becomes three times as large. What is the ratio of the new power dissipated in the resistor, P₂, to the original power, P₁?

options.text: P₂/P₁ = 3
P₂/P₁ = 6
P₂/P₁ = 9
P₂/P₁ = 1

questions.explanation: The resistor is ohmic, so R is unchanged. P = I²R: tripling I multiplies P by 3² = 9.

questions.stem: A student wants to measure the current in a lamp and the pd across it, but connects the meters the wrong way round. The circuit is: a cell, a voltmeter and the lamp connected in series in a single loop, with an ammeter connected in parallel with the lamp. Both meters are ideal. What does the student observe?

options.text: The lamp is off and both meters read zero, as there is no current in the circuit.
The lamp is off, the ammeter reads zero and the voltmeter reads the emf of the cell.
The ammeter short-circuits the lamp, so a very large current flows through the ammeter.
The lamp lights normally, and the meters show its current and pd as when correctly connected.

questions.stem: Predict first. A cell has an emf of 1.5 V. What does this mean?

options.text: The cell holds a store of 1.5 C of charge, which it releases into the circuit.
The cell pushes each coulomb of charge around the circuit with a force of 1.5 N.
For each coulomb passing through the cell, 1.5 J is transferred to electrical energy.
The cell drives a current of 1.5 A through any circuit connected to it.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp are both designed to work on the same 230 V supply. Which lamp has the larger resistance when working normally, and why?

options.text: The 100 W lamp, as a higher power needs a larger resistance.
Both are the same, as they are designed for the same supply pd.
The 60 W lamp, as at the same pd a smaller R gives more power.
The 100 W lamp, as P = I²R and it takes the larger current.

questions.explanation: At the same pd, P = V²/R. R = 230²/60 ≈ 880 Ω for the 60 W lamp and 230²/100 ≈ 530 Ω for the 100 W lamp.

questions.stem: In the series test, a student puts ammeters before and after two resistors: they read 0.25 A and 0.24 A. Voltmeters across the resistors read 2.1 V and 3.8 V, and across the supply 6.0 V. Which is the best conclusion?

options.text: Current is used up in the first resistor: 0.01 A is lost.
The pds do not add up, so energy is lost in the wires.
Within uncertainty, the current is the same everywhere and the pds add up to the supply pd.
The meters must be faulty, so the readings should be discarded.

questions.explanation: Right. 0.25 A and 0.24 A agree within meter uncertainty, and 2.1 + 3.8 = 5.9 V ≈ 6.0 V. Both series rules are confirmed.

questions.stem: A 60 W lamp and a 100 W lamp are both rated for a 230 V supply. They are connected in series across a 230 V supply. Assume each keeps its normal working resistance. Which lamp is brighter?

options.text: The 60 W lamp: it has the larger resistance, and in series both carry the same current.
The 100 W lamp: it has the higher power rating, so it gives more light.
The 100 W lamp: a smaller resistance gives more power, as P = V²/R.
Both are equally bright, as they carry the same current.

questions.explanation: R = V²/P: about 880 Ω for the 60 W lamp, 530 Ω for the 100 W lamp. Same current in series, so P = I²R is larger in the 60 W lamp (about 23 W against 14 W).

questions.stem: Three circuits are each made from an identical cell of negligible internal resistance, a resistor and a lamp. In circuit 1 the three form a single closed loop. Circuit 2 is the same loop with an open switch added. Circuit 3 is the same loop as circuit 1 with a wire of negligible resistance connected directly across the lamp's terminals. Which ranks the currents I₁, I₂ and I₃ in the lamps of circuits 1, 2 and 3?

options.text: I₁ > I₂ = I₃
I₁ = I₃ > I₂
I₃ > I₁ > I₂
I₁ = I₂ = I₃

questions.stem: Three identical lamps are connected to a supply of negligible internal resistance: lamp A is in series with lamps B and C, which are in parallel with each other. The filament of lamp C breaks. What happens to the brightness of lamps A and B? (Assume each lamp's resistance stays the same.)

options.text: A and B both go out, because the circuit is now broken.
A becomes dimmer and B becomes brighter.
A stays the same and B becomes brighter, because B now carries C's current.
A becomes brighter and B stays the same, because the parallel branch keeps its potential difference.
